Approvals only work if the agent tells Bentomux about them. Bentomux ships a hook script that agents load from their own settings file — install it once from Settings > Agents. Install is idempotent. Running it twice does not duplicate the entries. Hooks Bentomux did not write are never touched. Uninstall removes exactly what was added, and restores any values that were changed from Bentomux's own defaults. When a prompt arrives, Bentomux raises a small always-on-top window over everything else. It shows what the agent wants, and offers three answers: Approve — the agent continues. Deny — the agent is told no. Jump to tab — brings the pane that is asking to the front, for when you want to look before deciding. The window is resizable and remembers its size. A chime plays with the prompt; both the sound and the notification can be turned off in Settings. If the bridge cannot be reached, approval fails open — the agent is not left blocked on a prompt nobody can see. A plugin is a directory of JavaScript that adds buttons, panels, tabs, modals and background services to the app. Plugins A plugin is a directory of JavaScript that adds buttons, panels, tabs, modals and background services to the app.

Two files minimum: a JSON manifest and an ES module entry point. my-plugin/ plugin.json index.js { "id": "acme.my-plugin", "name": "My Plugin", "version": "0.1.0", "apiVersion": 1, "entry": "index.js", "permissions": ["storage"], "contributes": { "commands": [{ "id": "acme.my-plugin.hello", "title": "My Plugin: Hello" }] } } The entry exports an activate(ctx) function. ctx is the only handle you get — commands, storage, and the surfaces you declared. Your id must look like publisher.plugin in lowercase. The bentomux publisher is reserved. The validator runs from a terminal — no need to open the app. Exit 0 is clean, 1 means errors, 2 is a usage mistake. bentomux --plugin-validate ./my-plugin bentomux --plugin-validate ./my-plugin --json It checks, without running any of your code: the manifest exists, parses, and matches the schema the id is well formed and not using the reserved publisher version and minAppVersion are semver, apiVersion is known the entry file exists, is inside the plugin root, and is not empty every contribution id is namespaced under your plugin id and unique every permission name is one the app knows every command referenced by a button, sidebar entry or dock item is declared icons resolve — a builtin name, or a file that exists every network origin is a bare https:// host with no path the whole plugin is under 5 MB The CLI additionally runs node --check on the entry to catch syntax errors. The in-app validator skips that step, because Node is not guaranteed at runtime; a syntax error surfaces at activation instead. Settings > Remote. It is off by default. Turning it on generates a pairing token and a QR code — scan it with a phone and the monitor opens in that browser. The port defaults to 8765 and is changeable if something else on your network already has it. The token is generated once and kept, so paired devices survive a restart. Turning it on Settings > Remote. It is off by default. Turning it on generates a pairing token and a QR code — scan it with a phone and the monitor opens in that browser. The port defaults to 8765 and is changeable if something else on your network already has it. The token is generated once and kept, so paired devices survive a restart.

The local server binds to loopback only. It is never exposed to your network directly. Instead Bentomux runs a bundled cloudflared quick tunnel, which gives it a public https://trycloudflare.com URL. That URL, with the token embedded, is what the QR encodes — there is nothing else to type. The tunnel is end-to-end encrypted and the server refuses plain HTTP. Screen text is rendered headlessly, so what you see on the phone is the pane's actual contents with escape sequences already consumed. A PTY dies with whoever holds its master file descriptor. When that was the app itself, quitting Bentomux closed the fd, the kernel hung up the slave, and every agent CLI in every pane took a SIGHUP . So the master fds live somewhere else. The first time you open a pane, Bentomux launches itself a second time as a background daemon and talks to it over a loopback socket. bentomux --pty-host The daemon publishes its port and a shared secret in an owner-only address file, and speaks newline-delimited JSON over the socket. Quitting, crashing, or force-quitting the app now leaves your agent CLIs running. The next launch asks the daemon which terms are still alive and reattaches to the same processes — the same pids, not respawns. The pty host A PTY dies with whoever holds its master file descriptor. Bentomux is not tmux, and it does not pretend to be. Three things it does not do: No reattach from another terminal. The daemon speaks to the app over a loopback socket with a local-only secret. Attach from a second machine or a plain shell: not supported. No history replay. Reattaching restores the live screen, not a recording. Close the tab and its shell is gone — scrollback lives in the terminal emulator and dies with the pane. No server-side layout. The layout is your state file, not a session the daemon owns. Layout and preferences live in a single JSON file in the app data directory, as bentomux.json . It records your workspaces, your tabs, and the split tree inside each tab — which pane sits where, in which direction, and how the borders were dragged. The file is written by the app. Edit it while Bentomux is closed, or the next write overwrites you. Exact locations are in Configuration .
